claims.text: High-temperature plastic strain in fusion plasma-facing structural materials is primarily governed by the stability and distribution of nanoscale grain-boundary precipitates.
High-temperature toughness in fusion plasma-facing structural materials is primarily governed by the stability and distribution of nanoscale grain-boundary precipitates.
Nanoscale precipitates mediate dislocation motion and grain-boundary sliding.
Optimizing precipitate size, spacing, and coherence enhances dynamic recovery.
Optimizing precipitate morphology impedes premature grain coarsening.
Optimizing precipitate morphology increases high-temperature toughness and ductility.
A tailored heat-treatment or thermomechanical process can refine and distribute nanoscale precipitates uniformly along grain boundaries.
The relevant structural mediator is nanoscale precipitates decorating grain boundaries and subgrain regions.
Refined precipitate distributions stabilize grain boundaries by pinning dislocations.
Refined precipitate distributions limit grain-boundary sliding or dynamic recrystallization.
Precipitate-mediated grain-boundary stabilization enhances plastic deformation before failure.
Precipitate-mediated stabilization retards high-temperature embrittlement associated with grain growth.
Precipitate-tailored materials will exhibit significantly greater plastic strain than the baseline.
Precipitate-tailored materials will exhibit significantly higher impact or fracture toughness than the baseline.
The intervention will produce a finer and more uniform precipitate distribution with reduced grain coarsening.
A conventional, coarser, or less uniform precipitate population leads to lower high-temperature ductility and toughness.
The hypothesis is expected to apply at approximately 800–1200 °C.
The hypothesis is most relevant to refractory alloys and tungsten-based systems in which precipitate-induced stabilization affects high-temperature performance.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome refers to increased 'plastic strain before yield,' whereas the experiment measures plastic strain to failure. Plastic strain is ordinarily defined after yielding, so the stated prediction and measured endpoint are not aligned.
